text.p: Shares in Europe's top defence electronics maker Thomson-CSF fell on Tuesday after the new left-wing French government scrapped its privatisation.
Shares in one of the firm's suitors, missiles conglomerate Lagardere, also fell but engineering firm Alcatel Alsthom was buoyed by market speculation it might be given a minority role.
The government repeated on Tuesday that no decisions had been taken on potential alliances for Thomson-CSF as the cabinet weighs the next steps in a long-running privatisation saga.
In the market's first reaction to Friday's cancellation following a holiday weekend, 58-percent state-owned Thomson-CSF fell by more than four percent to 162.5 francs, down 7.1 francs.
Lagardere initially dropped 3.9 percent but clawed back some of the losses to show a 2.5 percent decline at 174.5 francs.
Shares in Alcatel Alsthom rose 1.7 percent to 778 francs.

Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's Socialist-led government, elected in June, said on Friday it was scrapping the privatisation launched by its centre-right predecessors because it was neither in the national nor the staff's interests. It said it would soon launch a new process aimed at creating a French industry giant with a "decisive" public stake.
That prompted weekend press reports that Alcatel, which had put in an entirely French bid, would be allowed in as a minority partner in an expanded defence industry group.
"No choice has been made regarding Thomson, as far as the operator itself is concerned nor as far as alliances to be made are concerned," a spokesman for Jospin said on Tuesday.
"There is no pre-decision. That would run counter to the rules and procedures," he said.
Alcatel and Lagardere were also the rival bidders in a previous failed attempt to privatise state parent company Thomson SA last year.
That attempted sale, which Lagardere had been poised to win, had to be dropped after criticism of plans to sell Thomson SA's subsidiary Thomson Multimedia to South Korea's Daewoo Group .
Lagardere on Monday described the latest press speculation about Alcatel's chances as premature and said similar reports had been proved wrong last year.

Thomson-CSF, which makes missile parts, radars and avionics, is Europe's leading defence equipment supplier with 46,000 worldwide staff and annual sales above 36 billion francs ($6 billion). ($ = 6.031 French Francs)
